Cascade-Aware Multi-Agent Routing:
Spatio-Temporal Sidecars and Geometry-Switching

Davide Di Gioia Email: ucesigi@ucl.ac.uk
March 2026
Abstract

A common architectural pattern in advanced AI reasoning systems is the symbolic graph network: a collection of specialized agents or modules connected by typed delegation edges, routing tasks through a dynamic execution graph. Agent orchestration frameworks, modular reasoning pipelines, and self-improving multi-agent engines are all instances of this pattern, and they share a structural blind spot. Their schedulers optimize load and fitness, but carry no model of how failure propagates differently depending on whether the current execution graph is tree-like, cyclic, or mixed. In tree-like delegation regimes, a single agent failure cascades exponentially through the hierarchy; in dense cyclic regimes, the same failure self-limits within one hop. A geometry-blind scheduler cannot distinguish these cases. This paper identifies the blind spot, quantifies its cost, and proposes a lightweight mitigation. Prior geometry-aware graph methods assume a static dataset with a fixed structural regime; multi-agent routing methods optimize delegation without modeling geometry or failure propagation. Neither addresses the runtime question: as the execution graph shifts between structural regimes under churn and noise, how should a route-risk estimator choose its geometric prior?

We cast this as adaptive geometry selection on a time-indexed execution graph with route-local failure propagation. Our model combines: (i) a Euclidean spatio-temporal baseline, (ii) a hyperbolic route-risk model with temporal decay and an optional repeat-failure burst-excitation term inspired by self-exciting point processes, and (iii) a learned geometry selector over structural graph features. The selector is a compact multilayer perceptron (9→12→19\to 12\to 1) whose inputs combine six topology statistics with three geometry-aware features: breadth-first search (BFS) shell-growth slope, cycle-rank norm, and fitted Poincaré curvature. On the heterogeneous benchmark, the learned selector resolves the principal failure mode of fixed hyperbolic models: in the hardest non_tree regime it improves win rate from 6464–72%72\% for fixed hyperbolic variants to 92%92\%, while achieving 87.2%87.2\% overall win rate across all stress conditions on the Genesis 3 benchmark distribution. A preliminary cross-architecture study on Barabási–Albert, Watts–Strogatz, and Erdős–Rényi graphs (Appendix I) confirms that structural propagation modeling generalises perfectly to all three families; the trained geometry gate requires retraining for out-of-distribution topologies.

To quantify total system value, we also evaluate Genesis 3 routing without any spatio-temporal sidecar, using only the signals available to the native bandit/LinUCB scheduler: team fitness and mean node load. This native baseline achieves 50.4%50.4\% win rate overall and only 20%20\% in tree-like regimes (clean and noise). Adding the full sidecar recovers 87.2%87.2\% overall, a +36.8+36.8 percentage-point system-level gain. In tree-like regimes the gain reaches +48+48 to +68+68 points, matching the prediction of our cascade-sensitivity analysis (Proposition 4): when graph expansion is exponential, node load alone does not reveal propagation risk.

The paper identifies geometry-blindness as a failure-propagation observability gap in execution-graph agent systems, not previously characterized to our knowledge across the dynamic-graph, multi-agent routing, or agent systems literature. It formalizes the gap as an online geometry-control problem, isolates its operational cost through a system-level ablation (50.4%50.4\% vs 87.2%87.2\% win rate), instantiates a solution with a compact learned geometry selector, and grounds the findings in a cascade-sensitivity analysis whose regime predictions match the empirical curves. The results support a general principle: execution-graph agent systems require a geometry-aware failure-propagation signal at the scheduling layer, and a 133133-parameter sidecar substantially mitigates this gap in at least one high-capability instance.

1 Introduction

A prevailing approach to building advanced AI reasoning systems is, at its core, symbolic graph network construction. Agent orchestration frameworks (e.g., LangGraph, AutoGen [1], CrewAI), modular reasoning pipelines, mixture-of-experts routing layers, and self-improving multi-agent engines all share the same fundamental architecture: agents are nodes, delegation relationships are directed edges, and executing a task means routing a signal through a time-varying graph. The same structure appears in the leading neuro-symbolic AGI research systems: AlphaGeometry [3] routes reasoning through a geometric construct graph; OpenCog Hyperon [2] stores all knowledge as a metagraph and runs every cognitive operation as graph-rewriting over it. This convergence on graph-structured execution is not accidental — graphs are the natural representation for distributed reasoning.

But this architectural consensus creates a shared, unexamined blind spot. No matter how sophisticated the individual agents, the scheduler that routes tasks through the graph is geometry-blind: it sees node load and agent fitness, but it does not model how the current shape of the graph determines how a single agent failure propagates. In tree-like delegation regimes, one failure cascades exponentially through the BFS shell structure: the failure amplification grows with depth. In dense cyclic regimes, the same failure self-limits within one or two hops. The scheduler cannot tell the difference. Any execution-graph system in this paradigm that routes tasks without a geometry-aware failure-propagation signal carries this observability gap, silently.

We make that blind spot concrete, measure its operational cost, and close it. Genesis 3 is a self-improving multi-agent reasoning engine whose execution graph shifts between tree-like, cyclic, and mixed regimes as its agent team evolves; it is the system in which we measure and fix the problem. The geometry-blind native scheduler achieves only 50.4%50.4\% overall win rate and 20%20\% in tree-like regimes. Adding a spatio-temporal sidecar with adaptive geometry selection recovers 87.2%87.2\% overall, a +36.8+36.8 percentage-point gain that is consistent with the theoretical prediction of our cascade-expansion analysis (Proposition 4). Genesis 3 is the measurement context; the structural argument generalizes to the class by construction via the geometry-blind definition and Proposition 4, and cross-architecture empirical validation is a direct avenue for future work (see Section 10).

The question we address is:

Given any symbolic-graph-network AI system whose execution graph shifts between tree-like, cyclic, and mixed regimes, how should a route-risk estimator choose its geometric prior at runtime?

To our knowledge, this question is not posed in prior work. Geometry papers assume a fixed dataset with a chosen structural regime. Multi-agent routing papers optimize scheduling and coordination without modeling graph geometry or failure propagation. Neither addresses the geometry-control problem that arises in any geometry-blind scheduler within the symbolic-graph-network paradigm, a common failure mode, we argue, across this architectural class, though broad cross-system empirical confirmation remains future work.

We study this problem in Genesis 3, a self-improving multi-agent reasoning system with routing, delegation, governance, and episodic traces. We introduce a spatio-temporal route-risk sidecar that evaluates active routes using time-indexed graph snapshots and failure events. Our contribution is fivefold:

  1. 1.

    Blind spot identification. We identify geometry-blindness as a failure-propagation observability gap common to execution-graph systems in contemporary agent orchestration: any system that routes tasks through a dynamic execution graph using a geometry-blind scheduler is systematically exposed to failure cascades whenever the graph enters a tree-like regime. We demonstrate and quantify this vulnerability empirically in Genesis 3 as a first instance; by construction, the structural argument applies to any system of this class that lacks runtime geometry monitoring, and we conjecture the finding extends to agent orchestration frameworks, modular reasoning pipelines, and self-improving multi-agent engines more broadly. Cross-architecture empirical validation is planned future work.

  2. 2.

    Problem formulation. We formalize the resulting gap as an online geometry-control problem for live execution graphs, distinct from both static geometry selection and standard MAS routing.

  3. 3.

    System-level baseline. We provide a system-level ablation showing that Genesis 3 routing without any failure-propagation model achieves only 50.4%50.4\% win rate overall (2020–40%40\% in tree-like regimes), quantifying the cost of the blind spot.

  4. 4.

    Instantiation. We instantiate the problem with a hyperbolic spatio-temporal model and a learned geometry selector (9→12→19\to 12\to 1 MLP, 133133 parameters), recovering a tied-best 87.2%87.2\% overall win rate and 92%92\% in the hardest non-tree regime on the Genesis 3 benchmark distribution. On out-of-distribution graph families without retraining, the structural propagation baseline generalises perfectly while the trained gate’s win rate ranges from 7%7\% (BA tree-like) to 65%65\% (WS small-world), confirming that the trained gate is distribution-specific (Appendix I).

  5. 5.

    Theoretical grounding. We prove that regime-specific failure dynamics (Proposition 4) predict where and why geometry-aware scoring adds value, with empirical results consistent with the theoretical prediction.

The operational question is whether a compact structural gate can predict, from graph features alone, which geometry will produce the larger route-separation margin on the current scenario. The gate is a meta-learner over a geometry-choice policy: it predicts which scoring geometry performs better on the current route, not which geometry is “true” for the graph in a generative sense.

To make the evaluation scientifically explicit, the paper tests three research questions. RQ1: does explicit failure-propagation modeling improve routing quality relative to the native scheduler signal alone? RQ2: under topology regime shift, does adaptive geometry selection outperform any fixed geometric prior? RQ3: do the observed gains occur in precisely the regimes predicted by cascade-expansion theory? The remainder of the paper is organized to answer these questions in that order.

1.1 Hypotheses

  • •

    H1 (Perception-gap hypothesis). Adding explicit failure-propagation modeling to native multi-agent routing improves safer-route selection relative to load-and-fitness-only routing.

  • •

    H2 (Regime-adaptation hypothesis). Under topology regime shift, a learned geometry selector outperforms any fixed geometric prior in held-out route-risk estimation.

  • •

    H3 (Theory-alignment hypothesis). The largest gains from the sidecar occur in high-expansion tree-like regimes, as predicted by cascade-expansion analysis.

2 Related Work and Gap

The present work lies at the intersection of four literatures: geometric graph representation learning, spatio-temporal graph learning, temporal point processes, and multi-agent communication or orchestration. Each contributes an important ingredient, but none directly studies the question posed here: how should a live multi-agent execution system choose its geometric prior as its topology shifts between hierarchical, cyclic, and mixed regimes?

2.1 Geometric Graph Learning

Hyperbolic representation learning is now a standard tool for graphs with latent hierarchy. Early work on hyperbolic neural networks showed that negatively curved spaces can represent tree-like growth far more efficiently than Euclidean spaces, especially when distances expand exponentially with depth [9]. This perspective was extended to graphs by hyperbolic graph convolutional networks, which demonstrated strong advantages on hierarchical and scale-free relational structure [5]. More generally, mixed-curvature models argued that no single constant-curvature manifold is universally adequate, and that different latent factors may be better represented in Euclidean, spherical, or hyperbolic components [19]; and constant-curvature GCN variants confirmed that the choice of curvature sign materially affects downstream task performance [4].

These papers establish a crucial baseline: geometry matters. However, geometry is typically chosen once for a dataset, architecture, or embedding space. The problem is static model selection, not online geometry control. Even work that expands the geometry family beyond pure hyperbolic space still assumes a fixed representational choice during training and evaluation. Our setting differs because the graph itself is not stationary: the same system may exhibit strongly hierarchical routes in one interval and dense reciprocal motifs in the next. The scientific question is therefore not only which geometry is expressive, but when each geometry should be preferred.

Recent dynamic-hyperbolic work also does not close this gap. For example, hyperbolic variational graph models for dynamic graphs show that non-Euclidean latent spaces can improve time-evolving graph modeling [22], and temporal hyperbolic embedding methods have been proposed for discrete-time dynamic networks [26]. These are important precedents, but they still optimize a chosen non-Euclidean family rather than treat geometry selection itself as the prediction problem.

2.2 Spatio-Temporal and Dynamic Graph Learning

The spatio-temporal graph learning literature studies signals or interactions evolving over graph structure. Canonical traffic-forecasting models such as DCRNN [14], STGCN [27], and Graph WaveNet [24] combine graph propagation with temporal modeling to capture diffusion, recurrence, and long-range dependencies. More recent dynamic-graph methods such as DyRep [23], Temporal Graph Networks [18], EvolveGCN [16], and temporal attention models [25] focus on continuous-time or event-driven representation learning on evolving graphs.

This line of work is highly relevant because our execution graph is explicitly time-indexed and the risk signal depends on both topology and history. However, these methods usually assume that the graph-learning architecture is fixed in advance. They answer questions such as how to encode time, how to update node states, or how to predict future edges or labels. They do not ask whether the underlying geometric prior should itself switch as topology changes. In that sense, our paper is adjacent to spatio-temporal graph learning, but its main object is a different one: regime-aware geometric bias for route-risk estimation.

Survey work on dynamic graphs makes this distinction clearer. Surveys of representation learning for dynamic graphs document a large space of temporal embedding methods, recurrent updates, attention mechanisms, and streaming adaptations [13]. Yet even in this broader perspective, the dominant assumption remains that a chosen geometry and message-passing family are fixed parts of the model class. Our work inserts a new decision layer on top of that assumption.

2.3 Temporal Point Processes and Self-Excitation

Our failure model also draws on temporal point-process reasoning. Hawkes processes introduced the foundational idea that past events can increase the short-term intensity of future events, thereby modeling clustered or self-exciting dynamics [10]. This idea has become central in event-sequence modeling, including recurrent marked temporal point processes [7] and neural Hawkes processes [15]. Reviews of self-exciting spatio-temporal point processes further show how excitation mechanisms are used in domains where localized events propagate over time and space [17].

We do not present a new point-process model in this paper. Rather, we use a lightweight burst-excitation heuristic inspired by self-exciting point processes as one ingredient inside route-risk scoring for repeated local failures. The gap relative to the point-process literature is therefore not temporal dependence per se; it is the coupling of temporally clustered failures with graph geometry selection in a live execution system.

2.4 Multi-Agent Communication and Orchestration

The multi-agent literature provides the systems motivation. Work on learned communication and coordination has shown that message passing, selective communication, and graph-structured interaction can substantially improve cooperative behavior [21, 6, 12]. There is also a long systems lineage on coordination, blackboard control, and distributed problem solving, where the execution graph is an operational object governing delegation and synchronization rather than a geometric object [11, 8].

These papers are close in spirit because they study how agents exchange information over changing interaction structures. But their central objectives are policy learning, communication efficiency, or coordination quality. They generally do not build a spatio-temporal route-risk estimator whose inductive bias changes with topology. In particular, we are not aware of prior work that takes a live execution graph from a multi-agent reasoning engine, models timestamped failure propagation on active routes, and treats geometry choice as a runtime decision variable.

The most directly relevant recent work in this space is Kim et al. [20] (Google Research, Google DeepMind, and MIT), who conduct a controlled large-scale evaluation of five canonical multi-agent coordination topologies across 180 configurations and derive quantitative scaling laws for agent systems. Their key empirical finding on topology-dependent error amplification is striking: independent-agent coordination amplifies errors 17.2×\times, while centralized coordination contains this to 4.4×\times. A predictive coordination model using topology-class and task-property features achieves cross-validated R2=0.524R^{2}=0.524. This is the strongest existing empirical evidence that coordination structure determines failure propagation magnitude in real multi-agent systems, and it directly motivates the concern we formalize. However, their analysis operates at design time: topology is a fixed architectural choice made before deployment, and the scaling model predicts which fixed topology to select. It does not model the intra-episode structural shifts that occur as a live execution graph moves between tree-like, cyclic, and mixed regimes during a single solve. Their 17.2×\times amplification figure is an aggregate over entire benchmark runs; it does not indicate when within a run the high-amplification condition exists, nor does it equip the scheduler with a live signal to detect that condition at route-scoring time. Our work addresses exactly this runtime perception gap: a geometry-aware cascade risk estimator that operates continuously as execution-graph topology evolves, providing the intra-episode structural monitoring layer that Kim et al. [20] leave open.

Many contemporary reasoning systems (agent orchestration frameworks and neuro-symbolic proof systems alike) execute by routing computation through an evolving graph of components and dependencies. This motivates our focus on execution-graph regime shifts and their operational consequences for routing. While prior work emphasizes expressiveness and search efficiency, our contribution isolates a complementary systems concern: route selection requires propagation-aware structural perception, and the appropriate geometric inductive bias can change online as the execution topology changes.

Definition 1 (Geometry-blind routing).

Consider a system that selects among candidate routes r∈ℛtr\in\mathcal{R}_{t} at time tt using a scoring rule

score⁡(r,t)=f⁡(ψt​(r),ξt),\mathrm{score}(r,t)=f\!\left(\psi_{t}(r),\,\xi_{t}\right),

where ψt​(r)\psi_{t}(r) are route-level aggregate observables (e.g. mean/max load, latency, cost, historical fitness) and ξt\xi_{t} are task/context features. We say the routing is geometry-blind if the scoring rule does not depend on any propagation-sensitive structural representation of the current execution graph, i.e. it does not use any feature map ϕ​(Gt​[r])\phi\!\left(G_{t}[r]\right) that measures expansion, cyclicity, or hyperbolicity of the subgraph induced by route rr (e.g. BFS shell-growth rate, cycle rank, Gromov δ\delta-hyperbolicity, or treewidth diagnostics), and does not simulate or estimate failure propagation on Gt​[r]G_{t}[r].

Equivalent characterization. Routing is geometry-blind if and only if, conditional on (ψt​(r),ξt)\left(\psi_{t}(r),\xi_{t}\right), the routing decision is invariant to any structural modification of Gt​[r]G_{t}[r] that preserves those aggregate observables.

2.5 Gap Statement

The gap can therefore be stated precisely. Hyperbolic and mixed-curvature learning show that geometry matters for graph structure. Spatio-temporal and dynamic-graph models show that time-varying graphs require temporal reasoning. Temporal point processes show that repeated failures can be self-exciting. Multi-agent systems show that execution graphs are operationally meaningful and can shift rapidly with workload. What prior work does not directly articulate, to our knowledge, is the following:

A dominant paradigm in contemporary agent orchestration (symbolic graph networks in which agents are nodes, delegation relationships are edges, and task execution is a routing problem on an evolving graph) produces the following failure-propagation observability gap in any system of this class that lacks runtime geometry monitoring: the scheduling layer is geometry-blind. It cannot distinguish tree-like regimes (where failure cascades exponentially) from cyclic regimes (where failure self-limits). This gap arises by construction from the geometry-blind definition, not from any quirk of a single implementation; we conjecture it is a structural property of the architectural class, though broad cross-system empirical confirmation remains future work. Many systems in this paradigm that route without geometry-aware propagation signals are likely to inherit this observability gap; we test and quantify it in Genesis 3.

The closest existing line of work combines dynamic hyperbolic embeddings with architectures that blend or compare multiple representational biases over temporal graphs. Those methods are the nearest conceptual neighbors because they acknowledge both time variation and geometry mismatch. However, they treat geometry as a model-class choice made offline, not as a runtime control variable inside a live execution system that is continuously restructuring its own agent graph. The vulnerability we identify is therefore not visible to these methods: they do not inspect the running execution graph at route-scoring time.

Prior work does not identify geometry-blindness as a failure-propagation observability gap in execution-graph agent systems, nor provide a runtime mechanism to close it. The individual components (hyperbolic structure, dynamic graphs, and temporally clustered failure signals) are each well established; the contribution is their integration into a runtime geometry-control layer inside a live multi-agent scheduler. Because this execution pattern is common to agent orchestration frameworks and modular reasoning pipelines, the observability gap is a natural failure mode for systems in this class that route without geometry-aware failure-propagation signals.

3 Problem Formulation

3.1 System Context: Genesis 3

Genesis 3 is a multi-agent reasoning engine in which a team of specialized agents (planners, generators, critics, and verifiers) collaborate to solve tasks through a 9-gate self-modification pipeline (syntax check →\to Bayesian proof →\to adversarial stress →\to Lean4 formal verification →\to ephemeral sandbox →\to causal validation, followed by canary and constitutional governance). This section gives the concrete interpretation of the abstract model that follows; readers familiar with multi-agent systems can map directly from model to implementation.

Nodes and edges.

Each node v∈Vtv\in V_{t} is an active agent instance: a software process (planner, generator, critic, or verifier) that accepts a task payload, executes one step of the reasoning pipeline, and emits outputs or delegates subtasks. Agents are organized into an AgentTeam with a directed acyclic communication-flow graph; the AgentTeamOrchestrator executes them in topological order, running parallel groups concurrently via a ThreadPoolExecutor. Each directed edge (u,v)∈Et(u,v)\in E_{t} is a task-delegation dependency, meaning that agent uu may pass work downstream to agent vv during a solve episode. Node load ℓt​(v)∈[0,1]\ell_{t}(v)\in[0,1] is a normalized occupancy fraction; edge weight wt​(u,v)w_{t}(u,v) reflects recent message-delivery reliability estimated from logs. The graph GtG_{t} changes over time as agents are spawned or decommissioned (churn) and as workload patterns shift.

Routes.

A route r=(v1,v2,…,vk)r=(v_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{k}) is an ordered delegation chain: agent v1v_{1} receives the original task and may delegate to v2v_{2}, and so on. The active route subgraph Gt​[r]G_{t}[r] contains exactly those kk agents and the directed edges among them. A new route is selected at each solve episode (one call to solve(problem, context)); routing decisions therefore occur at the frequency of task arrivals. The 9-gate pipeline creates deep sequential dependencies within a solve episode, which means that a failure at one gate may propagate forward and block all downstream stages unless an alternative delegation path exists: the key motivation for failure-propagation modeling.

Failures.

A failure event is logged whenever an agent raises an unhandled exception, times out, or produces output rejected by a downstream verifier. Each event is recorded as (τi,vi,si,ci,ri)(\tau_{i},v_{i},s_{i},c_{i},r_{i}) where τi\tau_{i} is the timestamp, viv_{i} is the affected agent, si∈[0,1]s_{i}\in[0,1] is a severity score derived from error type and downstream impact, cic_{i} is a category label (e.g., timeout, logic_error, gate_fail), and rir_{i} is the active route at the time. The failure history ℱ\mathcal{F} accumulates these events across episodes and is shared via a Blackboard (thread-safe shared memory).

Native scheduler.

Without the spatio-temporal sidecar, Genesis 3 selects routes using a LinUCBTuner: a contextual bandit with 9 route-configuration arms and a 6-dimensional context vector (5 task-context features plus a bias term). The reward signal is based on the team fitness score (exponentially smoothed success rate for the candidate route) and the mean node load ℓ¯\bar{\ell} over the route. This is adequate for steady-state load balancing but carries no failure-propagation model and no geometric prior, so it cannot distinguish tree-like delegation chains from dense cyclic ones under churn and noise. The sidecar in this paper is additive: it computes a supplementary route-risk score R⁡(r,t)R(r,t) that the scheduler can incorporate alongside its native signal.

3.2 Abstract Model

We model a running system as a time-indexed sequence of directed graphs

𝒢={Gt=(Vt,Et,wt,ℓt):t∈ℝ≥0},\mathcal{G}=\{G_{t}=(V_{t},E_{t},w_{t},\ell_{t}):t\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\},

where VtV_{t} is the active agent set, EtE_{t} is the communication or dependency edge set, wtw_{t} denotes edge reliability or strength, and ℓt\ell_{t} denotes node or edge load metadata.

Let a route rr at time tt activate a subgraph

Gt​[r]=(Vt​[r],Et​[r]).G_{t}[r]=(V_{t}[r],E_{t}[r]).

Let the failure history be a set of timestamped events

ℱ={(τi,vi,si,ci,ri)}i=1N,\mathcal{F}=\{(\tau_{i},v_{i},s_{i},c_{i},r_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N},

where τi\tau_{i} is time, vi∈Vτiv_{i}\in V_{\tau_{i}} is the affected node, si∈ℝ≥0s_{i}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} is severity, cic_{i} is event category, and rir_{i} is an optional route label.

The task is to construct a route-risk score

R⁡(r,t)∈ℝR(r,t)\in\mathbb{R}

that predicts vulnerability of the active route under future failure propagation.

The central difficulty is that the correct geometric inductive bias is itself time-dependent. We therefore introduce a geometry variable

gt​(r)∈{Euc,Hyp},g_{t}(r)\in\{\mathrm{Euc},\mathrm{Hyp}\},

or more generally a soft selector

πt​(r)∈[0,1],\pi_{t}(r)\in[0,1],

interpreted as preference for hyperbolic geometry.

The problem is to learn or estimate πt​(r)\pi_{t}(r) from graph structure and recent event history.

4 Spatio-Temporal Route-Risk Model

4.1 Temporal Failure Intensity

For node vv at time tt, define the temporally decayed failure intensity

λt(v;r)=∑i:vi=v,τi≤t([ri∈{∅,r}]siexp(−t−τih)α(ci)),\lambda_{t}(v;r)=\sum_{i:v_{i}=v,\;\tau_{i}\leq t}\Bigl(\mathbbm{1}\!\left[r_{i}\in\{\varnothing,r\}\right]\;s_{i}\;\exp\!\left(-\frac{t-\tau_{i}}{h}\right)\;\alpha(c_{i})\Bigr),

where h>0h>0 is a half-life parameter and α⁡(ci)\alpha(c_{i}) is a category-dependent multiplier.

The hyperbolic model can further augment this base intensity with a same-node burst term derived from successive inter-event gaps. Let mv=mv(t;r):=|{i:vi=v,ri∈{∅,r},τi≤t}|m_{v}=m_{v}(t;r):=|\{i:v_{i}=v,\;r_{i}\in\{\varnothing,r\},\;\tau_{i}\leq t\}| be the count of relevant events at node vv on route rr up to time tt, and let

τ(1)<τ(2)<⋯<τ(mv)\tau_{(1)}<\tau_{(2)}<\cdots<\tau_{(m_{v})}

be the corresponding ordered failure times.

Define the gap-based burst statistic

bt​(v,r)={1mv−1​∑q=1mv−1exp⁡(−τ(q+1)−τ(q)δ),mv≥2,0,mv<2,b_{t}(v;r)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{1}{m_{v}-1}\sum_{q=1}^{m_{v}-1}\exp\!\left(-\dfrac{\tau_{(q+1)}-\tau_{(q)}}{\delta}\right),&m_{v}\geq 2,\\[4.30554pt] 0,&m_{v}<2,\end{cases}

where δ>0\delta>0 is an excitation-decay constant. The damped implementation then uses

λ~t​(v,r)=λt​(v,r)+0.14​bt​(v,r)​st​(v,r)​dt​(v,r)​ot​(v,r),\tilde{\lambda}_{t}(v;r)=\lambda_{t}(v;r)+0.14\,b_{t}(v;r)\,s_{t}(v;r)\,d_{t}(v;r)\,o_{t}(v;r),

with

st(v;r)=tanh(λ¯t(v;r)),dt(v;r)=mv−1/2,ot(v;r)=11+max⁡{0,λt​(v,r)−λ0},s_{t}(v;r)=\tanh\!\left(\overline{\lambda}_{t}(v;r)\right),\qquad d_{t}(v;r)=m_{v}^{-1/2},\qquad o_{t}(v;r)=\frac{1}{1+\max\{0,\lambda_{t}(v;r)-\lambda_{0}\}},

where

λ¯t​(v,r):=1mv​∑q=1mvs(q)​exp⁡(−t−τ(q)h)​α​(c(q))\overline{\lambda}_{t}(v;r):=\frac{1}{m_{v}}\sum_{q=1}^{m_{v}}s_{(q)}\,\exp\!\left(-\frac{t-\tau_{(q)}}{h}\right)\,\alpha\bigl(c_{(q)}\bigr)

denotes the mean decayed severity of same-node events included in the base intensity. Here λ0=1\lambda_{0}=1 is the implementation’s baseline excitation threshold. The overload factor ot​(v,r)o_{t}(v;r) activates when the decayed base intensity exceeds λ0\lambda_{0}, indicating unusually concentrated recent failure mass. The benchmark also includes a classic ablation that replaces the damped term by 0.25∑q=1mv−1exp(−(τ(q+1)−τ(q))/δ)0.25\sum_{q=1}^{m_{v}-1}\exp\!\left(-(\tau_{(q+1)}-\tau_{(q)})/\delta\right). This is not a full Hawkes intensity; it is a bounded burstiness bonus based on local inter-arrival times, which is the quantity the implementation actually computes.

4.2 Euclidean Route Propagation

The Euclidean baseline propagates node-local risk over the route subgraph with diffusion, recovery, latency, and bottleneck penalties. If xt​(v)x_{t}(v) is the node risk, one step of propagation is abstractly of the form

xt+1​(u)=(1−ρu)​xt​(u)+∑(v,u)∈Et​[r]ηv​u​xt​(v),x_{t+1}(u)=\bigl(1-\rho_{u}\bigr)\,x_{t}(u)+\sum_{(v,u)\in E_{t}[r]}\!\eta_{vu}\,x_{t}(v),

where ρu\rho_{u} is adaptive recovery and ηv​u\eta_{vu} absorbs diffusion strength, load, latency, reliability, and route-local amplification.

The Euclidean route score is then a weighted combination of infected mass, frontier risk, tail risk, latency penalty, and bottleneck pressure.

4.3 Hyperbolic Route Propagation

The hyperbolic model embeds nodes into a Poincaré ball parameterized by curvature magnitude κ>0\kappa>0, corresponding to sectional curvature −κ-\kappa:

zt​(v)∈𝔹κd,𝔹κd:={z∈ℝd:∥z∥<1/κ}.z_{t}(v)\in\mathbb{B}^{d}_{\kappa},\qquad\mathbb{B}^{d}_{\kappa}:=\bigl\{z\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:\lVert z\rVert<1/\sqrt{\kappa}\bigr\}.

We score routes using hyperbolic geodesic quantities. The implementation uses:

  1. 1.

    curvature fitting from graph-structure stress,

  2. 2.

    time-decayed failure intensities,

  3. 3.

    tangent-space risk injection,

  4. 4.

    hyperbolic message passing,

  5. 5.

    route scoring by geodesic compactness, tail risk, frontier spread, and curvature-weighted bottleneck pressure.

In high-level form,

RHyp​(r,t)=[w1​Ct​(r)−w2​Tt​(r)−w3​Ft​(r)−w4​Bt​(r)+w5​Dt​(r)],R_{\mathrm{Hyp}}(r,t)=\bigl[w_{1}C_{t}(r)-w_{2}T_{t}(r)-w_{3}F_{t}(r)-w_{4}B_{t}(r)+w_{5}D_{t}(r)\bigr],

where CtC_{t} is compactness, TtT_{t} is tail risk, FtF_{t} is frontier spread, BtB_{t} is bottleneck pressure, and DtD_{t} is decoder consistency.

5 Adaptive Geometry Selection

5.1 Structural Features

We define a structural feature map

ϕ⁡(Gt​[r])∈ℝ9,\phi(G_{t}[r])\in\mathbb{R}^{9},

consisting of six original topology statistics and three new geometry-aware features.

Feature computation domain.

Global topology features (ϕ1\phi_{1}, ϕ2\phi_{2}, ϕ3\phi_{3}, ϕ7\phi_{7}, ϕ8\phi_{8}) are computed on the full snapshot graph GtG_{t}. Route-local features (ϕ4\phi_{4}, ϕ5\phi_{5}) are computed on the active route subgraph Gt​[r]G_{t}[r]. ϕ6\phi_{6} is the ratio of route node count to total node count in GtG_{t}. ϕ9\phi_{9} is derived from the curvature κ^\hat{\kappa} fitted to the full snapshot by golden-section search on graph-distance stress.

Original six features.

  • •

    ϕ1\phi_{1}: edge-surplus ratio, (|E|−(|V|−1))/|V|(|E|-(|V|-1))/|V|.

  • •

    ϕ2\phi_{2}: reciprocal ratio, the fraction of bidirectional edges.

  • •

    ϕ3\phi_{3}: triangle density, closed triplets divided by possible triplets.

  • •

    ϕ4\phi_{4}: route crosslink ratio, excess route-local edges divided by route |V||V|.

  • •

    ϕ5\phi_{5}: route load mean, mean node load over the active route.

  • •

    ϕ6\phi_{6}: route length norm, route |V||V| divided by total |V||V|.

Three geometry-aware features.

  • •

    ϕ7\phi_{7}: shell-growth slope γ^\hat{\gamma}. We identify roots as nodes with no incoming directed edges in GtG_{t}; if none exist, the first node in the adjacency map is used. Starting from those roots, BFS is run following directed edges, assigning each reachable node to its earliest-reached depth kk. Nodes not reachable from any root are placed in a fallback layer at depth maxk+1\max_{k}+1; this ensures ∑k|Vk|=|Vt|\sum_{k}|V_{k}|=|V_{t}| and limits distortion from disconnected components to at most one additional data point in the OLS fit. In the tree-like and near-tree regimes where γ^\hat{\gamma} is most diagnostic, unreachable mass is typically negligible. We count layer sizes |Vk||V_{k}| and fit

    ln⁡(|Vk|+1)=a+γ^​k\ln\!\left(|V_{k}|+1\right)=a+\hat{\gamma}\,k

    over all layers by ordinary least squares, then set ϕ7=tanh⁡(max⁡(0,γ^))∈[0,1]\phi_{7}=\tanh\!\Bigl(\max\bigl(0,\hat{\gamma}\bigr)\Bigr)\in[0,1]. When γ^\hat{\gamma} is large, the graph expands exponentially with depth, the regime where hyperbolic embeddings achieve low distortion relative to Euclidean models [9].

  • •

    ϕ8\phi_{8}: cycle-rank norm,

    ϕ8=|Eundirected|−|Vt|+Ct|Vt|,\phi_{8}=\frac{|E_{\mathrm{undirected}}|-|V_{t}|+C_{t}}{|V_{t}|},

    where |Eundirected||E_{\mathrm{undirected}}| counts undirected edges of the full snapshot GtG_{t} and CtC_{t} is the number of connected components in the full undirected snapshot graph. This is the normalized dimension of the cycle space. It is zero for trees and grows monotonically with cyclicity.

  • •

    ϕ9\phi_{9}: fitted curvature norm,

    ϕ9=κ^−0.104.50−0.10∈[0,1].\phi_{9}=\frac{\hat{\kappa}-0.10}{4.50-0.10}\in[0,1].

    After fitting the Poincaré-ball curvature κ^\hat{\kappa} to graph-distance stress via golden-section search, the fitted value itself encodes how much the snapshot deviates from flat space.

The full feature map is therefore

ϕ=(ϕ1,…,ϕ6⏟topology statistics,ϕ7,ϕ8,ϕ9⏟geometry-aware),\phi=(\underbrace{\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{6}}_{\text{topology statistics}},\underbrace{\phi_{7},\phi_{8},\phi_{9}}_{\text{geometry-aware}}),

with each component normalized to [0,1][0,1].

5.2 Geometry Gate

The selector is a two-layer multilayer perceptron

πt​(r)=σ⁡(W2​ReLU⁡(W1​ϕ​(Gt​[r])+b1)+b2),\pi_{t}(r)=\sigma\!\Bigl(W_{2}\,\operatorname{ReLU}\!\left(W_{1}\phi(G_{t}[r])+b_{1}\right)\;+\;b_{2}\Bigr),

with architecture 9→12→19\to 12\to 1 (133133 parameters), He initialization, mini-batch gradient descent, and sigmoid output. The scalar πt​(r)\pi_{t}(r) is interpreted as a soft hyperbolic preference.

The final route-risk score may be written as a soft mixture

R⁡(r,t)=[πt​(r)​RHyp​(r,t)+(1−πt​(r))​REuc​(r,t)],R(r,t)=\bigl[\pi_{t}(r)\,R_{\mathrm{Hyp}}(r,t)+\bigl(1-\pi_{t}(r)\bigr)\,R_{\mathrm{Euc}}(r,t)\bigr],

or as a hard selection rule after thresholding πt​(r)\pi_{t}(r).

We also compute gate uncertainty via binary entropy,

H⁡(π)=−π​log⁡π−(1−π)​log⁡(1−π),H(\pi)=-\pi\log\pi\;-(1-\pi)\log\!\bigl(1-\pi\bigr),

which is maximal near π=1/2\pi=1/2 and minimal near deterministic selections.

5.3 What Is Theoretically Justified by the Implemented Gate

The current selector is a discriminative preference model, not a latent-variable mixture estimator. In the implementation, the gate is trained on binary labels indicating which geometry achieves the larger route-separation margin on a scenario. Concretely, the training target is

Y=[MHyp(r,t)≥MEuc(r,t)],Y=\mathbbm{1}\!\left[M_{\mathrm{Hyp}}(r,t)\geq M_{\mathrm{Euc}}(r,t)\right],

where MHypM_{\mathrm{Hyp}} and MEucM_{\mathrm{Euc}} denote the route-separation margins induced by the hyperbolic and Euclidean scoring pipelines, respectively. In code, this objective is optimized through the equivalent sigmoid-plus-binary-cross-entropy output-layer gradient ∂ℓ/∂z=p−y\partial\ell/\partial z=p-y rather than by explicitly materializing the scalar loss at each step. The gate therefore learns a conditional preference probability from structural features rather than identifying a hidden mixture coefficient from observed outputs alone.

The implemented training objective is empirical binary cross-entropy:

θ^∈arg⁡minθ​1n​∑j=1n(−Yj​log⁡(πθ​(ϕj))−(1−Yj)​log⁡(1−πθ​(ϕj))),\hat{\theta}\in\arg\min_{\theta}\;\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\Bigl(-Y_{j}\,\log\!\left(\pi_{\theta}(\phi_{j})\right)\;-(1-Y_{j})\,\log\!\left(1-\pi_{\theta}(\phi_{j})\right)\Bigr),

where (ϕj,Yj)(\phi_{j},Y_{j}) are labeled training scenarios and πθ\pi_{\theta} denotes the selector network.

Proposition 1 (Structural Preference Recoverability).

Let ϕ⁡(Gt​[r])∈ℝ9\phi(G_{t}[r])\in\mathbb{R}^{9} be the structural feature map used by the selector, and define the margin difference

Δ⁡(ϕ)=MHyp​(ϕ)−MEuc​(ϕ).\Delta(\phi)=M_{\mathrm{Hyp}}(\phi)-M_{\mathrm{Euc}}(\phi).

Assume there exists a measurable decision rule

g⋆(ϕ)=[Δ(ϕ)≥0]g^{\star}(\phi)=\mathbbm{1}\!\left[\Delta(\phi)\geq 0\right]

such that |Δ⁡(ϕ)|≥δ|\Delta(\phi)|\geq\delta for some δ>0\delta>0 on a set of positive probability. Then any sufficiently expressive discriminative gate trained on labeled pairs (ϕ,Y)(\phi,Y) can recover the geometry-preference rule g⋆g^{\star} up to estimation error.

Proof sketch.

By construction, Y=g⋆​(ϕ)Y=g^{\star}(\phi) almost surely. The margin-gap assumption |Δ⁡(ϕ)|≥δ|\Delta(\phi)|\geq\delta away from the zero-margin set rules out arbitrarily unstable labels on that set and therefore yields a well-defined Bayes classifier. A discriminative hypothesis class with sufficient approximation power can approximate this classifier, and empirical risk minimization over labeled pairs (ϕ,Y)(\phi,Y) recovers it up to the usual estimation error terms determined by sample size and model capacity. ∎

Proposition 2 (Calibrated Preference Probability).

Let

η⁡(ϕ)=ℙ⁡(Y=1∣ϕ)\eta(\phi)=\mathbb{P}(Y=1\mid\phi)

denote the conditional probability that hyperbolic scoring outperforms Euclidean scoring on the route-separation objective. If the gate class is rich enough to approximate η\eta and training minimizes binary cross-entropy over i.i.d. labeled examples, then the learned output πt​(r)\pi_{t}(r) estimates a calibrated geometry-preference probability up to estimation error.

Proof sketch.

Binary cross-entropy is a strictly proper scoring rule. Its population minimizer over measurable predictors is therefore the conditional class probability η⁡(ϕ)\eta(\phi). Consequently, when the network class can represent η\eta exactly or to small approximation error, minimizing empirical binary cross-entropy yields a predictor whose output is calibrated to the event that hyperbolic scoring outperforms Euclidean scoring on the benchmark objective, again up to estimation error. ∎

These propositions do not claim that the selector identifies an underlying latent geometry variable in a generative sense. They claim something narrower and algorithmically faithful: the selector can learn a stable, probabilistic geometry preference rule from structural observables.

5.4 What the Benchmark Actually Evaluates

The benchmark does not ask the gate to recover an unobserved latent geometry variable. Instead, it constructs supervised labels from comparative performance:

Y=[MHyp(r,t)≥MEuc(r,t)],Y=\mathbbm{1}\!\left[M_{\mathrm{Hyp}}(r,t)\geq M_{\mathrm{Euc}}(r,t)\right],

where each margin measures how well a scorer separates attacked from safe route footprints on the same scenario. The learned selector is therefore evaluated on a concrete prediction task:

  1. 1.

    observe the current structural feature vector ϕ​(Gt​[r])\phi(G_{t}[r]),

  2. 2.

    predict whether hyperbolic or Euclidean scoring will perform better on the route-separation objective,

  3. 3.

    use that probability as a soft routing weight,

  4. 4.

    measure the resulting margin on held-out scenarios.

This is a valid and meaningful experiment. It tests whether geometry preference is predictable from live structural signals, and whether exploiting that predictability improves route-risk estimation under regime shift. What it does not yet test is a stronger geometric theorem phrased directly in terms of distortion bounds, shell growth, or explicit hyperbolicity diagnostics.

To make the evaluation target mathematically explicit, let R^s​(r)\hat{R}_{s}(r) denote the route score returned by a given scorer on scenario ss. Then define the scenario-level margin as

Ms=R^s​(rsafe)−R^s​(rattacked),M_{s}=\hat{R}_{s}(r_{\mathrm{safe}})-\hat{R}_{s}(r_{\mathrm{attacked}}),

where a positive value means the scorer correctly assigns higher risk to the attacked route than the safe one. In the benchmark, each scenario presents two routes drawn from the same snapshot graph GtG_{t}: the attacked route has synthetic failure events injected into its last three nodes with geometrically decreasing severity (0.850.85, 0.730.73, 0.610.61), timestamped 00–22 seconds before the scoring call; the safe route is an adjacent path in the same graph receiving no injections. Route pairs are assigned by even/odd indexing over the route enumeration of each snapshot, ensuring a single safe comparator per attacked route from the same structural and temporal context.

Define the win indicator as

Ws=[Ms>0].W_{s}=\mathbbm{1}\!\left[M_{s}>0\right].

Then overall mean margin and win rate are

M¯=1N​∑s=1NMs,W¯=1N​∑s=1NWs.\bar{M}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{s=1}^{N}M_{s},\qquad\bar{W}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{s=1}^{N}W_{s}.

These are the two reported evaluation statistics throughout Section 8.

6 Why a Fixed Geometric Prior Fails Under Regime Shift

6.1 Suboptimality of Fixed Priors

Proposition 3 (Suboptimality of Fixed Geometric Priors).

Suppose the execution-graph process visits at least two structural regimes with positive probability: one regime in which hyperbolic bias is strictly better for route-risk separation and one regime in which Euclidean bias is strictly better. Then any fixed geometric prior is suboptimal in expected risk-separation performance compared to an oracle regime-aware selector.

Proof sketch.

Let JHyp​(ρ)J_{\mathrm{Hyp}}(\rho) and JEuc​(ρ)J_{\mathrm{Euc}}(\rho) denote the expected route-separation objective under regime ρ\rho, and write ℛH={ρ:JHyp​(ρ)>JEuc​(ρ)}\mathcal{R}_{H}=\{\rho:J_{\mathrm{Hyp}}(\rho)>J_{\mathrm{Euc}}(\rho)\} and ℛE={ρ:JEuc​(ρ)>JHyp​(ρ)}\mathcal{R}_{E}=\{\rho:J_{\mathrm{Euc}}(\rho)>J_{\mathrm{Hyp}}(\rho)\}. By assumption, both sets have positive probability under the regime process. A fixed hyperbolic prior loses the positive excess term JEuc​(ρ)−JHyp​(ρ)J_{\mathrm{Euc}}(\rho)-J_{\mathrm{Hyp}}(\rho) on ℛE\mathcal{R}_{E}, while a fixed Euclidean prior loses the symmetric term on ℛH\mathcal{R}_{H}. An oracle that selects arg⁡max⁡{JHyp​(ρ),JEuc​(ρ)}\arg\max\{J_{\mathrm{Hyp}}(\rho),J_{\mathrm{Euc}}(\rho)\} pointwise avoids both losses, so its expected objective strictly dominates either fixed prior. ∎

6.2 Cascade Sensitivity to Graph Expansion

The deeper reason geometry matters is that failure dynamics depend directly on graph expansion rate. In hyperbolic space with curvature magnitude κ>0\kappa>0 (sectional curvature −κ-\kappa), the volume of a ball of radius rr grows as Vol⁡(r)∝eκ​r\mathrm{Vol}(r)\propto e^{\kappa r}, and correspondingly the number of nodes at BFS depth kk satisfies

|Vk|≈C​eγ​k|V_{k}|\approx Ce^{\gamma k}

for some expansion rate γ>0\gamma>0.

Proposition 4 (Cascade Sensitivity to Expansion).

Let a failure process propagate with probability pp per edge at each step on a graph whose BFS shell sizes satisfy |Vk|≈C​eγ​k|V_{k}|\approx Ce^{\gamma k}. Let NrN_{r} denote the number of newly affected nodes in BFS shell rr rather than the cumulative number affected up to depth rr. Then

𝔼⁡[Nr]≈pr​|Vr|≈C​e(γ+ln⁡p)​r.\mathbb{E}[N_{r}]\approx p^{\,r}\,|V_{r}|\approx C\,e^{(\gamma+\ln p)\,r}.

A cascade is supercritical when

γ+lnp>0⇔p>e−γ.\gamma+\ln p>0\qquad\Leftrightarrow\qquad p>e^{-\gamma}.
Proof sketch.

Under the shell-growth approximation, the number of candidate recipients in shell rr scales as |Vr|≈C​eγ​r|V_{r}|\approx Ce^{\gamma r}. If each forward transmission succeeds independently with probability pp, then the contribution of a depth-rr path is weighted by prp^{r}, so the expected newly infected mass arriving in shell rr scales as pr​|Vr|p^{r}|V_{r}|. Substituting the shell approximation yields

𝔼⁡[Nr]≈pr​C​eγ​r=C​e(γ+ln⁡p)​r.\mathbb{E}[N_{r}]\approx p^{r}Ce^{\gamma r}=Ce^{(\gamma+\ln p)r}.

The process is supercritical precisely when the exponent is positive, which is equivalent to p>e−γp>e^{-\gamma}. ∎

In a slowly expanding or dense cyclic graph (γ≈0\gamma\approx 0), the cascade threshold becomes p>1p>1, which is never satisfied under realistic propagation probabilities. In a strongly branching graph (large γ\gamma), the threshold is p>e−γ≪1p>e^{-\gamma}\ll 1 and cascades are easy to trigger. Thus,

  • •

    large γ\gamma (tree-like, hyperbolic regime) implies structurally dangerous propagation and favors hyperbolic route-risk scoring,

  • •

    small γ\gamma with high cycle rank (dense, Euclidean regime) implies self-limiting failures and makes Euclidean diffusion adequate.

The gate πt​(r)\pi_{t}(r) is therefore learning to detect whether the graph is in the supercritical cascade regime. The three geometry-aware features directly encode the relevant quantities: ϕ7\phi_{7} estimates γ\gamma, ϕ8\phi_{8} measures deviation from tree structure, and ϕ9\phi_{9} captures the fitted Poincaré curvature κ^\hat{\kappa}.

7 Experimental Setup

The evaluation uses the Genesis 3 sidecar benchmark with the following design:

  1. 1.

    250250 scenarios total,

  2. 2.

    243243 real traces,

  3. 3.

    train seeds 00–44, evaluation seeds 55–99,

  4. 4.

    source-separated reporting,

  5. 5.

    95%95\% percentile bootstrap confidence intervals with 400400 resamples for both mean margin and win rate,

  6. 6.

    comparators including Euclidean baseline, structural baseline, external networkx baseline, hyperbolic ablations, hand-designed geometry switching, and learned geometry switching.

The stress conditions include clean, noise, churn, mixed, and non_tree regimes.

For the learned selector, training labels are generated by comparing the hyperbolic and Euclidean route-separation margins on each training scenario. In the implemented benchmark, the learned gate is fit separately per trace group on training seeds 00–44 and evaluated on held-out seeds 55–99; the hyperbolic label source uses the fitted-curvature route scorer with decoder enabled and excitation disabled, matching the inference configuration of the learned selector itself. The resulting experiment is therefore a held-out test of geometry-preference prediction and soft geometry blending, not a direct test of an embedding-distortion theorem.

The benchmark emits two source-separated real-trace groups: planning_adapted and mixed_real. Because mixed_real contains the full real-trace corpus and therefore overlaps with planning_adapted, the headline tables in this paper report the planning_adapted breakdown as the primary benchmarkable source, and use the broader mixed_real group only as a robustness check. This avoids reporting pooled values that would otherwise reflect overlap-driven double counting. A fresh rerun under the multiagent environment reproduced the same headline point estimates used below and removed the earlier provenance concern associated with an external temporary-output file.

The experimental design is intended to answer the research questions stated in Section 1 with minimal ambiguity. RQ1 is answered by the system-level ablation against Genesis 3 native routing without the sidecar. RQ2 is answered by comparing learned switching against fixed Euclidean and fixed hyperbolic variants under held-out evaluation seeds. RQ3 is answered by the stress-regime breakdown, which tests whether the largest gains occur in high-expansion tree-like settings and whether the gains contract in dense cyclic settings where Proposition 4 predicts self-limiting cascades.

Throughout, we report both mean margin and win rate because they capture different operational properties. Mean margin measures the average separation induced by a scorer; win rate measures the probability of selecting the safer route on a scenario. For deployment-facing routing claims, we treat win rate as the primary decision metric and mean margin as a complementary robustness diagnostic. Bootstrap confidence intervals and source-separated reporting are included to reduce over-interpretation of pooled averages. These intervals are descriptive resampling summaries over scenarios, not pairwise hypothesis tests between models; we therefore use them to characterize uncertainty, not to claim formal significance from interval overlap alone.

The bootstrap unit is the scenario, that is, the episode-level benchmark instance after route scores have already been aggregated within that scenario. We therefore resample scenarios with replacement rather than individual routing decisions inside a scenario. This keeps the resampling unit aligned with the reported margin and win statistics and avoids overstating effective sample size when multiple internal route computations contribute to one episode summary.

For the headline system-level comparison between Genesis 3 native routing and learned switching, we additionally report an exact paired sign test on per-scenario wins. This supplements the descriptive bootstrap intervals with one formal paired test while remaining faithful to the episode-level evaluation unit.

Reproducibility.

The benchmark divides into two components. Synthetic: (i) failure events injected into benchmark scenarios follow a fixed severity schedule (0.850.85, 0.730.73, 0.610.61) with timestamps set 00–22 seconds before each scoring call; (ii) the BA/WS/ER cross-architecture suite (Appendix I) uses standard networkx generators with n=7n=7, m=1m=1 (BA), k=2k=2, p=0.3p=0.3 (WS), p=0.5p=0.5 (ER) and seeds 00–1919; (iii) the feature-ablation suite (Appendix J) uses hand-coded team topologies with seeds 00–1919. Trace-derived: the 243243 planning traces in the primary benchmark are extracted from live Genesis 3 solve episodes and are not independently releasable at this time. The gate is trained on seeds 00–44 and evaluated on seeds 55–99 (main benchmark) or seeds 00–99 / 1010–1919 (Appendix J). All tables in the synthetic appendices can be reproduced from the parameter values above; main-benchmark results additionally require access to a Genesis 3 instance. Benchmark scripts and the synthetic suite will be released alongside any accepted version of this paper.

8 Results

8.1 Overall Results

The Genesis 3-native ablation row is new and provides the system-level anchor. Every model above it in Table 1 includes failure-propagation modeling. The +36.8+36.8 point gap between the Genesis 3-native baseline (50.4%50.4\%) and the learned selector (87.2%87.2\%) is the total value delivered by the entire spatio-temporal sidecar. The learned selector ties the structural baseline on win rate but achieves a substantially larger mean margin (0.38460.3846 vs. 0.26650.2665), which is the stronger evidence that adaptive geometry is improving separation quality rather than matching the baseline by chance on binary wins alone. The hand-designed switching row provides a direct ablation: it blends geometry weights via cycle-rank fraction alone with fixed coefficients and no learned parameters, achieving 82.4%82.4\% win rate and mean margin 0.25450.2545. The learned MLP exceeds it by +4.8+4.8 percentage points in win rate and +51%+51\% in mean margin, confirming that the parametric gate adds material value beyond the simplest threshold-rule alternative.

On the primary planning_adapted breakdown, the fresh multiagent rerun reports bootstrap intervals of [−0.0393,−0.0085][-0.0393,-0.0085] for the Genesis 3-native mean margin and [40.8%,59.2%][40.8\%,59.2\%] for its win rate, versus [0.3406,0.4398][0.3406,0.4398] and [81.6%,93.6%][81.6\%,93.6\%] for learned switching. The substantial separation in both mean-margin and win-rate intervals is consistent with a large system-level effect, while still remaining a descriptive uncertainty summary rather than a formal pairwise significance test.

Evaluation protocol robustness.

A natural concern is whether the sidecar’s advantage is an artefact of the original attack-footprint design (which ranks attacked nodes partly by failure severity, potentially correlating with node load). Appendix F repeats the evaluation under three alternative attack-node selection protocols. The cleanest probe is the adversarially uncorrelated random protocol, where attacked nodes are chosen uniformly at random with no correlation to node load or failure severity. Under this protocol the native baseline wins 54.4%54.4\% of scenarios; the sidecar wins 78.8%78.8\%, a +24.4\mathbf{+24.4} pp gap attributable solely to propagation modeling. The sidecar win rate is stable across all three protocols (69.669.6–88.8%88.8\%) while the native baseline varies widely (53.253.2–100%100\%), confirming that the main-benchmark result is not an artefact of footprint alignment. We highlight this result here rather than leaving it solely to the appendix, as it directly addresses the most common evaluation-design objection to route-risk benchmarks.

Compared to the six-feature gate (6→8→16\to 8\to 1, topology statistics only, mean margin 0.36760.3676, win rate 86.4%86.4\%), adding the three geometry-aware inputs improves mean margin by +4.6%+4.6\% and win rate by +0.8+0.8 percentage points while maintaining the 92%92\% non-tree performance that is the paper’s primary contribution. This margin improvement is distribution-dependent: a controlled feature-ablation study on a homogeneous held-out set (Appendix J) finds Δ​margin=+0.0008\Delta\mathrm{margin}={+0.0008}, within bootstrap noise. The +4.6%+4.6\% gain on the main benchmark is a consequence of that benchmark spanning five topology regimes where ϕ7\phi_{7}–ϕ9\phi_{9} are informative; on evaluation distributions that do not cover those regimes, the geometry block adds no measurable signal.

8.2 Regime-Specific Results

The key results occur in the heterogeneous regimes.

These results support the claim that topology regime matters. Fixed hyperbolic priors perform well when the graph remains sufficiently tree-like, but adaptive geometry selection is materially better when cyclic and mixed structure appears.

The three new geometry-aware features (ϕ7\phi_{7}, ϕ8\phi_{8}, ϕ9\phi_{9}: shell-growth slope, cycle-rank norm, fitted curvature norm) do not change the qualitative finding but strengthen the gate’s representational capacity. In particular, the geometry-aware gate preserves the 92%92\% non-tree win rate of the six-feature gate while improving the overall mean margin from 0.36760.3676 to 0.38460.3846 and maintaining top-tier non-tree separation performance. The main effect of the added features is therefore not a new qualitative regime result, but a cleaner and more stable geometry-preference signal, one that is conditionally informative: it materialises on evaluation distributions spanning the full topology diversity of the main benchmark but reduces to noise-level on homogeneous distributions (Appendix J).

The fresh rerun also supports the regime-specific claims. In non_tree, learned switching attains mean margin 0.34040.3404 with CI [0.2750,0.3931][0.2750,0.3931] and win rate 92.0%92.0\% with CI [84.0%,98.0%][84.0\%,98.0\%]; in mixed, the corresponding values are 0.27510.2751 with CI [0.2296,0.3186][0.2296,0.3186] and 84.0%84.0\% with CI [74.0%,94.0%][74.0\%,94.0\%].

Structural signals in the live graph contain enough information to predict which geometry will perform better on held-out scenarios.

8.3 Geometry-Gate Diagnostics

To evaluate H2 directly rather than only through downstream routing outcomes, we measured the learned gate as a held-out classifier on evaluation seeds 55–99, where the label is

Y=[MHyp≥MEuc].Y=\mathbbm{1}\!\left[M_{\mathrm{Hyp}}\geq M_{\mathrm{Euc}}\right].

We measure calibration via Expected Calibration Error (ECE) and Maximum Calibration Error (MCE). Gate output probabilities are binned into B=10B=10 equal-width intervals on [0,1][0,1]. Within each non-empty bin bb, let p¯b\bar{p}_{b} denote the mean predicted probability and y¯b\bar{y}_{b} the fraction of positive labels; then

ECE=∑b=1B|ℬb|N|y¯b−p¯b|,MCE=maxb:|ℬb|>0|y¯b−p¯b|.\mathrm{ECE}=\sum_{b=1}^{B}\frac{|\mathcal{B}_{b}|}{N}\,\bigl|\bar{y}_{b}-\bar{p}_{b}\bigr|,\qquad\mathrm{MCE}=\max_{b:\,|\mathcal{B}_{b}|>0}\bigl|\bar{y}_{b}-\bar{p}_{b}\bigr|.

A well-calibrated predictor has ECE near zero; MCE captures the worst-case confidence–accuracy gap over any single bin.

On the full held-out set of 250250 scenarios, the gate achieves AUC 0.92470.9247, accuracy 86.4%86.4\%, ECE 0.06810.0681, and MCE 0.79980.7998 (MCE is a worst-bin statistic sensitive to sparse extreme-probability bins; AUC and ECE are the more stable summary diagnostics). The overall confusion matrix is (TP,TN,FP,FN)=(182,34,30,4)(\mathrm{TP},\mathrm{TN},\mathrm{FP},\mathrm{FN})=(182,34,30,4), showing that most thresholded mistakes are false positives rather than missed hyperbolic-win cases. This matters because it means the gate rarely fails to identify scenarios where hyperbolic scoring is actually better; its main error mode is over-selecting hyperbolic in some Euclidean-favorable cases.

The regime breakdown is also informative. Discrimination remains strong in clean (AUC 0.92260.9226), noise (0.94640.9464), non_tree (0.96350.9635), and mixed (0.93750.9375), while churn is the only materially degraded regime (AUC 0.72590.7259, ECE 0.12000.1200). The thresholded confusion matrices make the same point more concretely: non_tree yields (30,16,2,2)(30,16,2,2) and mixed yields (30,18,0,2)(30,18,0,2), whereas churn yields (38,0,12,0)(38,0,12,0), indicating that the current threshold almost always predicts hyperbolic there. In other words, the weak spot is not hidden by aggregate win rate; it is visible in the classifier diagnostics.

Entropy summaries provide a coarse regime-wise histogram of gate certainty. Overall, 46.0%46.0\% of held-out cases fall in a low-entropy band, 52.4%52.4\% in a medium-entropy band, and only 1.6%1.6\% in a high-entropy band. The gate is most decisive in mixed, where 100%100\% of cases are low-entropy, and in non_tree, where 64%64\% are low-entropy. By contrast, clean, noise, and churn are dominated by medium-entropy predictions, indicating that the gate remains discriminative there but with less margin from the decision boundary. These diagnostics show the gate is a direct predictor of geometry preference, not just a downstream routing correlate.

8.4 System-Level Ablation: Genesis 3 Without the Spatio-Temporal Layer

To establish the total system-level value of the sidecar, we include a baseline that simulates Genesis 3 routing without any failure-propagation model. This baseline scores a route as

score⁡(r)=fteam×(1−0.5×ℓ¯),\mathrm{score}(r)=f_{\mathrm{team}}\times(1-0.5\times\bar{\ell}),

where fteamf_{\mathrm{team}} is the bandit fitness score and ℓ¯\bar{\ell} is the mean node load over the active route.

The pattern is mechanistically explained. In tree-like regimes (clean/noise/churn), failure propagation amplifies exponentially through branches. Node load at steady state provides no signal about this vulnerability: a lightly loaded route can still sit atop a high-γ\gamma branching subgraph that will amplify any injected failure. The spatio-temporal sidecar detects this structural vulnerability through failure history and geometry; the native routing layer cannot. In non-tree and mixed regimes, the attacked-node subset happens to carry structurally higher load by construction, making the fitness-times-load signal accidentally informative. Here the sidecar adds little; the cascade threshold p>e−γp>e^{-\gamma} is regime-specific: large γ\gamma (tree-expanding graphs) makes cascades easy to trigger, and that is exactly the regime where the sidecar is indispensable.

The fresh confidence intervals reinforce that interpretation. In clean, Genesis 3-native achieves 20.0%20.0\% win rate with CI [10.0%,30.0%][10.0\%,30.0\%] while learned switching reaches 84.0%84.0\% with CI [74.0%,92.0%][74.0\%,92.0\%]; in noise, the corresponding values are 20.0%20.0\% with CI [10.0%,32.0%][10.0\%,32.0\%] versus 88.0%88.0\% with CI [78.0%,96.0%][78.0\%,96.0\%]; in churn, 40.0%40.0\% with CI [26.0%,54.0%][26.0\%,54.0\%] versus 88.0%88.0\% with CI [78.0%,96.0%][78.0\%,96.0\%]. By contrast, non_tree produces identical 92.0%92.0\% win rates with CI [82.0%,98.0%][82.0\%,98.0\%] for Genesis 3-native versus [84.0%,98.0%][84.0\%,98.0\%] for learned switching, and mixed shows only a small separation: 80.0%80.0\% with CI [68.0%,90.0%][68.0\%,90.0\%] for Genesis 3-native versus 84.0%84.0\% with CI [74.0%,94.0%][74.0\%,94.0\%] for learned switching. The uncertainty pattern therefore matches the mechanism claim rather than weakening it.

For the headline comparison, the exact paired sign test on per-scenario wins rejects the null of equal win probability. On the full held-out set, learned switching beats Genesis 3-native on 9898 discordant scenarios versus only 66 in the opposite direction (146146 ties), giving p=1.59×10−22p=1.59\times 10^{-22}. On the primary planning_adapted slice, the corresponding counts are 4949 versus 33 (7373 ties), giving p=1.04×10−11p=1.04\times 10^{-11}. We therefore retain the bootstrap intervals as descriptive summaries while also supplying a formal paired test for the main system-level claim.

9 Discussion

9.1 Why Fixed Geometry Fails

The main message is not that hyperbolic geometry is wrong. On the contrary, hyperbolic structure remains highly effective when the execution graph is hierarchical. The problem is that live multi-agent systems do not remain in one structural regime. As soon as dense feedback, reciprocal links, or mixed motifs appear, the fixed-prior assumption becomes fragile and performance becomes regime-dependent. Proposition 3 formalizes the core point: once the regime process visits both hierarchy-dominated and cycle-dominated states with positive probability, any static geometric prior incurs avoidable expected loss relative to a regime-aware selector.

9.2 Perception-Gap Hypothesis (H1)

The ablation in Section 8.3 shows that failure-propagation modeling is the dominant performance driver. In the tree-like clean, noise, and churn regimes, the native scheduler attains only 20%20\%, 20%20\%, and 40%40\% win rate, whereas the sidecar lifts those values to 84%84\%, 88%88\%, and 88%88\%. Without an explicit propagation model, Genesis 3 cannot perceive the structural difference between a lightly loaded but cascade-prone route and a genuinely safe route. Geometry selection becomes relevant only after this perception gap is closed.

9.3 Regime-Adaptation Hypothesis (H2)

Once propagation is modeled, the remaining question is whether geometry preference is predictable from the live structural state. The answer given by the held-out benchmark is yes: learned switching matches the best overall win rate and materially improves route-separation margin relative to the strongest fixed-prior structural baseline, while also recovering 92%92\% win rate in the hardest non_tree regime. The rerun now includes standalone held-out gate diagnostics. Across all 250250 scenarios, the gate’s positive-label rate is 74.4%74.4\%, AUC is 0.92470.9247, thresholded accuracy is 86.4%86.4\%, expected calibration error is 0.06810.0681, and mean predictive entropy is 0.33590.3359, with 46.0%46.0\% of cases in a low-entropy regime and only 1.6%1.6\% in a high-entropy regime. Regime-wise, discrimination remains strong in clean (AUC=0.9226\mathrm{AUC}=0.9226), noise (0.94640.9464), non_tree (0.96350.9635), and mixed (0.93750.9375), with a clear degradation only in churn (0.72590.7259; ECE 0.12000.1200). H2 is supported by both held-out routing outcomes and direct classification evidence. The reported maximum calibration error is larger (0.79980.7998 overall) because it is a worst-bin statistic and is sensitive to sparse extreme-probability bins; for that reason we treat AUC and ECE as the more stable summary diagnostics.

9.4 Margin, Win Rate, and Decision-Threshold Robustness

Table 1 shows that hyperbolic_no_excitation attains the highest mean margin (0.41230.4123) yet a lower win rate (79.2%79.2\%) than the learned selector (87.2%87.2\%). This apparent inconsistency has a clean explanation.

Why margin and win rate diverge.

Win rate measures the probability that a scorer correctly signs the route-risk comparison (Ms>0M_{s}>0). Mean margin measures the average magnitude of that signed score. A fixed hyperbolic model with high curvature produces large separations in regimes where hyperbolic geometry is appropriate (tree-like, large γ\gamma) while systematically misclassifying a fraction of scenarios in non-tree and mixed regimes where the geometric prior is mismatched. The result is a high mean margin (driven by strongly correct tree-like cases) combined with a lower win rate (penalized by the non-tree misclassifications). The learned gate is optimized on binary win labels Y=𝟙[MHyp≥MEuc]Y=\mathbbm{1}[M_{\mathrm{Hyp}}\geq M_{\mathrm{Euc}}] rather than on margin magnitude; it is therefore tuned to maximize the probability of the correct binary outcome, which produces the correct sign on more scenarios even when the separation magnitude in strongly tree-like cases is somewhat smaller. A familiar analogy: this is a precision–recall tradeoff, where the gate trades peak-margin headroom for better coverage across heterogeneous regimes.

Why win rate is the right primary metric.

In a routing context, the decision is binary: select route r1r_{1} or r2r_{2}. The consequence of an error scales with whether the safer route was selected, not with the magnitude of the cost-function score. The +7.2+7.2 percentage-point win-rate advantage of the learned gate over hyperbolic_no_excitation translates directly into fewer unsafe route selections per 100 episodes. Mean margin advantage would be the primary criterion only if the downstream cost function were proportional to score magnitude rather than binary correctness, which does not reflect the routing use-case. This is why win rate is treated as the primary decision metric throughout Section 8.

Threshold sensitivity.

The gate outputs a soft score πt​(r)∈[0,1]\pi_{t}(r)\in[0,1]; routing decisions are made by comparing blended route-risk scores R⁡(r,t)=πt​(r)​RHyp+(1−πt​(r))​REucR(r,t)=\pi_{t}(r)\,R_{\mathrm{Hyp}}+(1-\pi_{t}(r))\,R_{\mathrm{Euc}} for the two candidate routes. Gate diagnostics (Table 7) show that 46%46\% of held-out cases fall in the low-entropy (high-certainty) band and only 1.6%1.6\% in the high-entropy band, confirming that the gate is rarely near the decision boundary in practice. Varying the blending weight continuously and tracing the full margin–win-rate Pareto surface is a constructive further-work item. The current regime-stratified AUC results (0.920.92–0.960.96 in four of five regimes) confirm that gate discrimination is robust across structural regimes, not sensitive to a particular operating threshold.

9.5 Theory-Alignment Hypothesis (H3)

The largest gains appear exactly where Proposition 4 predicts them. In high-expansion tree-like regimes, the sidecar gains are +64+64 to +68+68 percentage points, which is the operational signature of the supercritical condition p>e−γp>e^{-\gamma}. In dense cyclic regimes, the native baseline is already strong because node load correlates with the failure footprint, and the sidecar adds only modest gains. The empirical regime pattern is therefore not a post hoc story; it is aligned with the expansion-based mechanism derived in Section 6.

9.6 Broader Implications

A routing layer may be paired with strong planning, delegation, or language capabilities and still underperform when its representation omits propagation-sensitive structure. The same applies in LLM orchestration stacks, automated trading pipelines, and similar latency-sensitive systems.

The gate’s compactness (133133 parameters) suggests structural-perception modules can be small, and it motivates the following future work directions: (i) asynthetic cross-architecture benchmark using Barabási–Albert trees, Watts–Strogatz small-world networks, and Erdős–Rényi dense graphs, matched on node count and load distribution, to verify that the regime-sensitivity gain generalises beyond Genesis 3’s trace distribution; (ii) runtime overhead characterisation of the sidecar as a latency-aware production component, including per-call latency and memory footprint; (iii) continuous curvature adaptation and online mixed-curvature control; and (iv) richer calibration analysis including reliability diagrams, threshold-sensitivity curves, and confidence intervals beyond the scalar diagnostics reported here.

10 Limitations

  • •

    L1: Single-system evaluation. All benchmarks are conducted within Genesis 3. No equivalent open multi-agent system with runtime topology regime shifts exists for external validation at the time of writing. This means we cannot yet claim that the problem or the sidecar generalizes across architectures. Response: the structural ablation makes the contribution claim falsifiable within the system, which is a necessary first step before cross-system comparison becomes possible. A preliminary synthetic cross-architecture study has been run using Barabási–Albert, Watts–Strogatz, and Erdős–Rényi graphs matched on node count and load distribution (300 scenarios, 20 seeds per family; Appendix I). The structural propagation baseline achieves 100%100\% win rate on all three families, confirming that the core finding (that failure-propagation modeling outperforms load-only routing) is not Genesis 3-specific. The trained geometry gate, without retraining, achieves 65%65\% win rate on Watts–Strogatz small-world graphs but only 7%7\% on BA tree-like and 46%46\% on ER dense-cyclic. Cross-architecture generalisation of the propagation principle is therefore robust; cross-architecture generalisation of the trained gate requires fine-tuning on the target graph family.

  • •

    L2: ARC trace limitations. The ARC episode source provides coverage-only traces with no failure events. It validates that the sidecar obtains topology snapshots correctly but cannot support the attack-separation benchmark. Response: we report sources separately and do not mix coverage-only and failure-benchmarkable traces. The 250250-scenario benchmark uses only planning traces with real failure events.

  • •

    L3: Ablation geometry in non-tree/mixed regimes. In non_tree and mixed regimes, the Genesis 3-native baseline achieves 92%92\% and 80%80\% win rate respectively because structural node load correlates with the attack footprint in dense graphs. Part of that correlation is mechanistic, but part is benchmark-induced: the attacked/safe footprint construction ranks candidate nodes by failure severity with node load as a secondary key, which gives the native load-based baseline partial alignment with the evaluation target in dense regimes. The sidecar therefore adds little in these regimes (+0+0 and +4+4 points). Response: this pattern is still consistent with Proposition 4, but the dense-regime ablation should be interpreted as conservative evidence for sidecar value rather than as an unbiased estimate of how often load-only routing would succeed under an independently defined attack footprint.

  • •

    L4: Peak mean-margin vs. win-rate tradeoff. The learned selector achieves a tied-best win rate (87.2%87.2\%) but does not dominate hyperbolic_no_excitation on mean margin (0.38460.3846 vs. 0.41230.4123). Response: in a routing decision, win rate is the operationally relevant metric. We report both and do not suppress the tradeoff.

  • •

    L5: Theoretical scope. Propositions 1, 2, 3, and 4 justify preference recoverability from observable features and establish the cascade-sensitivity mechanism. They do not prove a stronger result, such as latent-geometry identifiability in a generative sense or minimax optimality. Response: the implemented gate is a discriminative classifier, not a generative model; the propositions faithfully describe what is actually implemented.

  • •

    L6: Benchmark-diagnostic scope. The rerun now reports gate-level diagnostics such as AUC, accuracy, calibration error, and entropy stratified by regime, but it still stops at scalar summaries. We do not yet include reliability diagrams, threshold-sensitivity curves, source-group calibration slices, or confidence intervals for the diagnostics themselves. Response: this is enough to support H2 as a discriminative claim, but a submission-grade revision should expand the diagnostic section beyond summary statistics.

  • •

    L7: Novelty claim scope. All novelty claims are qualified as “to our knowledge.” A submission-quality version should undergo a venue-specific related-work pass to confirm no directly analogous formulation exists in unpublished or concurrent work.

11 Conclusion

We introduced an online geometry-control problem for live multi-agent execution graphs and demonstrated that runtime regime shifts make fixed geometric priors suboptimal for route-risk estimation.

Failure-propagation modeling.

A system-level ablation shows that Genesis 3 routing without any spatio-temporal sidecar achieves 50.4%50.4\% win rate overall and as low as 20%20\% in tree-like regimes, essentially indistinguishable from random. Team fitness and node load contain no signal about exponential failure spread through a branching subgraph. Any route-risk method that models propagation closes this gap: the full sidecar recovers 87.2%87.2\%, a +36.8+36.8 point system-level gain.

Adaptive geometry selection.

Once failure propagation is modeled, the additional question is which geometric prior to use. Fixed hyperbolic models collapse to 6464–72%72\% win rate in non-tree regimes; the learned geometry gate recovers 92%92\%. The gate is small (133133 parameters), learns from structural observables alone, and demonstrates that regime information is recoverable from live graph statistics without expensive search or large models.

Geometry in live multi-agent systems is a dynamic control variable, not a fixed representational assumption. The prerequisite for that adaptive layer is the failure-propagation modeling that makes route risk structurally observable. More broadly, structural perception limits agent system performance in ways distinct from reasoning quality and addressable independently.
