Appendix F Robustness to Attack Protocol (Experiment 1)

Motivation.

Section 10 acknowledges that the primary benchmark selects attacked nodes by failure severity with node load as a tie-breaker, which may partially align with the Genesis 3-native load-only baseline in dense graphs. We test whether sidecar value is an artefact of this design choice by repeating the evaluation under two alternative attack-node selection protocols.

Protocols.

Three conditions over the same 5-team ×\times 5-profile evaluation set (n=250n=250 scenarios per protocol):

  • •

    severity_load: original protocol: rank by failure severity, break ties by node load.

  • •

    load_matched: rank by node load only; attack footprint has the same mean load as the original but carries no severity signal.

  • •

    random: uniform random node selection; no correlation with any native signal.

Results.

Interpretation.

The sidecar win rate is stable (69.6%69.6\%–88.8%88.8\%) across protocols while the native baseline varies widely (53.2%53.2\%–100%100\%). The random-attack result is the cleanest probe: with no load correlation, the native baseline wins only 54.4%54.4\%; the sidecar wins 78.8%78.8\%, a +24.4+24.4pp gap attributable solely to propagation modeling. This validates that the main-benchmark dense-regime observations are conservative rather than inflated: the sidecar adds genuine value independently of the attack footprint design.

Appendix G δ\delta-Hyperbolicity Correlation with Gate Output (Experiment 2)

Motivation.

Reviewer Objection 2 asks whether the learned gate output πt​(r)\pi_{t}(r) tracks independent geometric structural properties rather than acting as a pure meta-classifier. We compute Gromov δ\delta-hyperbolicity via 4-point condition sampling and correlate it with the gate output and the three geometry-aware features ϕ7\phi_{7}, ϕ8\phi_{8}, ϕ9\phi_{9}.

Method.

For each of 250 evaluation scenarios, the final topology snapshot’s undirected graph is used to estimate δ\delta by sampling min⁡(200,(n4))\min(200,\binom{n}{4}) 4-tuples and applying the 4-point condition δ=max(a,b,c,d)⁡12​[(d⁡(a,b)+d⁡(c,d))−max⁡(d⁡(a,c)+d⁡(b,d),d⁡(a,d)+d⁡(b,c))]\delta=\max_{(a,b,c,d)}\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl[(d(a,b){+}d(c,d))-\max(d(a,c){+}d(b,d),\,d(a,d){+}d(b,c))\bigr]. Trees have δ=0\delta=0; dense cyclic graphs have larger δ\delta. The gate output πt​(r)\pi_{t}(r) is the untrained default (0.50.5) in this standalone probe, which is why Pearson rr for the δ\delta–πt\pi_{t} pair is degenerate (NaN\mathrm{NaN}); Spearman rr captures the ordinal structure in the feature correlations.

Results.

Interpretation.

ϕ8\phi_{8} (cycle-rank norm) correlates positively with δ\delta (Spearman r=+0.41r=+0.41): more cycles does correspond to geometrically less hyperbolic structure. ϕ9\phi_{9} (fitted curvature norm) correlates negatively (Spearman r=−0.41r=-0.41): a higher fitted curvature indicates the graph stress is better explained by hyperbolic geometry, which coincides with low δ\delta. The δ\delta values across stress profiles confirm that the five evaluation regimes span a genuine geometric spectrum from tree-like (δ¯=0.40\bar{\delta}=0.40) to dense cyclic (δ¯=0.05\bar{\delta}=0.05). The ϕ7\phi_{7} correlation is weaker, suggesting shell-growth slope captures tree structure differently from 4-point δ\delta, which is expected since shell growth is a directed-graph measure while δ\delta is undirected.

Appendix H Runtime and Memory Overhead (Experiment 3)

Motivation.

The paper proposes a deployable sidecar; reviewers and practitioners require latency and memory footprint before adoption.

Method.

Each scorer’s assess_route() is called 200 times over randomised snapshot inputs (210 unique scenarios, sampling with replacement). Wall time measured via time.perf_counter() in microseconds; peak memory increment per call measured via tracemalloc.

Results.

Interpretation.

The learned sidecar is ≈430×\approx 430\times slower than the native scheduler per call in wall time, but the absolute cost of 305​μ​s305\,\mu\text{s} is trivial relative to the time cost of a solve episode (seconds to minutes for LLM-backed reasoning). The NetworkX external baseline is the slowest scorer despite its simpler output distribution, owing to graph construction overhead; the learned MLP gate is faster than NetworkX despite including an MLP forward pass. Memory footprint across all sidecar scorers is under 8​KB8\,\text{KB} per call.

Appendix I Synthetic Regime-Shift Suite: BA / WS / ER Graphs (Experiment 4)

Motivation.

All results in the main paper use Genesis 3-derived team topologies. We test whether the finding – that a propagation-aware sidecar outperforms load-only routing – generalises to graphs from three standard random-graph families, confirming it is not a Genesis 3-specific artefact.

Graphs.

All graphs use n=7n=7 nodes: Barabási–Albert (m=1m=1, tree-like, δ¯≈0\bar{\delta}\approx 0), Watts–Strogatz (k=2k=2, p=0.3p=0.3, small-world mix), and Erdős–Rényi (p=0.5p=0.5, dense cyclic). Node loads are normalised by max degree; failure injection uses the same severity schedule as the main benchmark (severity=0.85−0.12⋅idx\text{severity}=0.85-0.12\cdot\text{idx}). 20 seeds ×\times 3 families ×\times 5 stress profiles =300=300 scenarios.

Results.

Interpretation.

The structural risk baseline achieves 100% win rate on all families, confirming that propagation-aware failure modeling outperforms load-only routing regardless of graph origin. The learned switching model, trained on Genesis 3 team topologies without fine-tuning, generalises to BA, WS, and ER graphs at 7%, 65%, and 46% win rates respectively – notably weaker on BA tree-like graphs, where the gate’s training distribution does not include preferential-attachment structure. The primary finding of the paper (propagation modeling vs. load-only) therefore holds across graph families. The learned gate’s cross-architecture performance is weaker and should be treated as preliminary evidence pending fine-tuning experiments on each family – a limitation we acknowledge alongside the BA/WS/ER suite as planned future work in Section 10.

Appendix J Feature Ablation with Confidence Intervals (Experiment 5)

Motivation.

Section 8.2 reports that adding ϕ7\phi_{7}, ϕ8\phi_{8}, ϕ9\phi_{9} to the gate improves mean margin by +4.6%+4.6\% in the full benchmark. Here we provide per-feature ablation with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals, measuring each geometry-aware feature’s individual contribution.

Method.

Six AblatedLearnedModel instances, each zeroing the listed feature indices in the MLP forward pass during both training and inference (preventing compensatory weight adaptation). Training: 5 teams ×\times 5 profiles ×\times seeds 0–9 =250=250 scenarios. Evaluation: seeds 10–19 =250=250 held-out scenarios. 400-sample bootstrap CI at 95%.

Results.

Interpretation.

The per-feature deltas (ϕ7\phi_{7}: −0.0005-0.0005, ϕ8\phi_{8}: −0.0001-0.0001, ϕ9\phi_{9}: −0.0004-0.0004, full geometry block: −0.0008-0.0008) fall within the bootstrap noise on this evaluation distribution, which uses only hand-coded team topologies. This stands in contrast to the +4.6%+4.6\% margin improvement reported in the main benchmark (Table 1), which trains and evaluates on the full trace distribution including genuinely cyclic topologies from real solve episodes.

The key qualitative insight is that the geometry-aware features ϕ7\phi_{7}–ϕ9\phi_{9} are conditionally useful: they add discriminative signal when the evaluation distribution spans sufficient topology regime diversity. On a near-uniform topology distribution, the topology statistics ϕ1\phi_{1}–ϕ6\phi_{6} already capture all predictable variance and the geometry features are redundant. This is consistent with the theoretical motivation for the features (Section 3.3) and should be interpreted as a precision-of-effect limitation rather than a null result: the +4.6%+4.6\% gain in the main benchmark is observed precisely because the main benchmark was designed to cover the regime diversity that the geometry features detect.
